pages.title: Lots
pages.content: We buy six green lots a year and keep four on the bar at a time. Kiamara (Nyeri, Kenya, 1,800 m, washed) €17, Alto Rocío (Huila, Colombia, 1,700 m, washed) €15, Hara Bura (Guji, Ethiopia, 2,000 m, natural) €16 and El Mirador (Chalatenango, El Salvador, 1,600 m, honey) €18, each per 200 g bag.

pages.title: Bar
pages.content: The bar is open Wednesday to Sunday, 8:00–16:00. Filter from the current lot is €4.50, espresso €3.00, cortado €3.80, flat white €4.20, a pour-over flight of two lots €8.00 and a cardamom bun €3.50.

pages.title: People
pages.content: Seven of us: Ines Duarte (head roaster, co-founder), Tomas Varga (green buyer, co-founder), Amara Okoye (roaster), Mei Lin Ho (quality and cupping), Lena Brandt (head barista), Rafael Souza (barista) and Joost de Wit (wholesale and deliveries).

pages.title: Roastery
pages.content: One 5 kg drum roaster, three mornings a week: Monday, Tuesday and Thursday from 6:30. Every Thursday at 11:00 Mei Lin Ho cups every roast of the week. Beans rest until day five and are poured at the bar until day twenty-eight.

pages.title: Visit
pages.content: Branderijstraat 12, 9000 Ghent, Belgium, five minutes’ walk from Gent-Dampoort station. Phone +32 9 000 12 34, hello@mamecoffee.example. Bar hours Wednesday to Sunday 8:00–16:00.

posts.title: A week at Hara Bura
posts.excerpt: Tomas Varga walks the hillside plots in Guji and watches natural processing on raised beds at harvest.
posts.content:
Tomas Varga spent a week in Guji, Ethiopia, walking the hillside plots of the farm that grows our Hara Bura lot. Cherries are picked ripe, laid out on raised mesh beds and turned by hand through the day so they dry evenly.

He came home with samples, notes and the same conclusion as every year: buy few lots, and know who grew them.

posts.title: Sorting by hand
posts.excerpt: New green arrivals are graded by density and sorted for defects before the drum is lit.
posts.content:
When a new lot of green coffee arrives in Ghent, we sort a sample by hand in a round sieve before it ever meets the drum. We look for broken beans, insect damage and anything that does not belong.

It takes an hour for a few hundred grams, and it tells us more about a harvest than any spreadsheet.

posts.title: Day 5 to day 28
posts.excerpt: Why we rest every roast for five days, and why each lot leaves the bar within twenty-eight.
posts.content:
Freshly roasted coffee is full of gas. We let every roast rest for five days before it is poured, so the cup is clear rather than foamy and sharp.

After four weeks the sweetness starts to fade. So each lot leaves the bar by day twenty-eight, whatever is left in the bag.
